title: Given a year, draw a flowchart to check whether it is a leap year. Start, read year, decision (year % 4 == 0 AND year % 100 != 0) OR (year % 400 == 0), Yes print Leap Year, No print Not a Leap Year, End. Input: 2000, Expected Output: Leap Year.
shortTitle: Leap Year — check whether a year is a leap year

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A year is a leap year in the Gregorian calendar when it is divisible by four, except that century years are not leap years unless they are also divisible by four hundred. Expressed as one condition, a year is leap when it is divisible by four and not divisible by one hundred, or when it is divisible by four hundred. The algorithm reads the year and evaluates this single compound boolean condition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India computes interest on Rajesh's deposit using the actual number of days in the year, which is three hundred sixty-six in a leap year and three hundred sixty-five otherwise, so the day-count convention needs to know whether a given year is a leap year. For the year two thousand, which is divisible by four hundred, the answer is leap, so interest uses three hundred sixty-six days.

**One line to remember:** A year is leap when it is divisible by four and not by one hundred, or divisible by four hundred, and this directly decides the day count used for interest.

sections.s2_technical:
The rule has three parts combined into one boolean expression. Divisible by four is the base rule. The exception removes century years, those divisible by one hundred, because most of them are not leap years. The exception to the exception restores century years that are divisible by four hundred, which are leap years. Written out, the condition is (year modulo four equals zero and year modulo one hundred is not zero) or (year modulo four hundred equals zero). If the whole expression is true the year is a leap year.

You can check this manually with modulo, and that is what the flowchart shows, but in production Java I would use `java.time.Year.of(year).isLeap()`, which implements the exact Gregorian rule and removes any chance of getting the operator precedence or the exceptions wrong. For example `Year.of(2000).isLeap()` returns true and `Year.of(1900).isLeap()` returns false. Relying on the standard library here is the senior choice because date rules are notoriously easy to get subtly wrong.

In banking this feeds day-count conventions for interest. An actual-over-actual convention uses the real number of days in the year, so leap-year detection changes the denominator from three hundred sixty-five to three hundred sixty-six, which changes the interest figure. A senior nuance is that different products use different conventions, such as thirty over three hundred sixty, and the leap-year rule only matters for the actual-days conventions, so I keep the day-count logic explicit and well tested, and I validate the year is sensible before using it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India computes interest using the actual number of days in the year, so it must know whether a given year is a leap year to use three hundred sixty-six days instead of three hundred sixty-five. This is exactly the leap-year compound condition.

Problem 2 — Century years are a trap: nineteen hundred is not a leap year but two thousand is, and getting this wrong misprices interest. This is exactly why the condition includes the divisible-by-one-hundred exception and the divisible-by-four-hundred exception to it.

Problem 3 — The rule is easy to implement incorrectly, so correctness must be guaranteed. This is exactly why production code delegates to the standard Year.isLeap method.

Our mini-project builds a `LeapYearService` with an `isLeapYear(int year)` method showing both the explicit condition and the standard-library check, and a `LeapYearDemo` runnable that reports two thousand as a leap year.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: year = 2000.

Step 1 — The year two thousand is read into the service after a validity check that it is positive.

Step 2 — The explicit condition evaluates its first part: two thousand modulo four is zero, true, but two thousand modulo one hundred is also zero, so the not-divisible-by-one-hundred part is false, making the first whole part false.

Step 3 — The second part evaluates two thousand modulo four hundred, which is zero, true. Since the two parts are joined by or, the overall condition is true.

Step 4 — The standard-library check Year.of(2000).isLeap also returns true, confirming the explicit result, and the method returns true.

Step 5 — Because the year is leap, the day count is set to three hundred sixty-six, and the result is logged for use in the interest calculation.

Final output:

```
2026-10-31 23:54:00 [INFO] 2000 is a Leap Year -> interest day count = 366
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: year = 2000
    │
    ▼
  (2000%4==0 AND 2000%100!=0)  → (true AND false) = false
            OR
  (2000%400==0)                → true
    │
    ▼
  overall = false OR true = TRUE
    │
    ▼
  leap = true → day count = 366
    │
    ▼
  Output: Leap Year, 366 days
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Leap Year Rule ═══

  ┌─ Principles ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: service only decides leap/day-count       │
  │  Delegate to Year.isLeap() — authoritative     │
  │  Keep explicit rule + assert for parity         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │        LeapYearService       │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + isLeapYear(year:int):bool  │ throws IllegalArgumentException
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for isLeapYear(year):
    Pre:  year >= 1
    Post: true iff (div by 4 and not 100) or div by 400
    Throws: IllegalArgumentException on year < 1

  Call Chain:
  1. isLeapYear(2000)
  2.   (2000%4==0 && 2000%100!=0) = false
  3.   2000%400==0 = true
  4.   false || true = true → return true
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A year is a leap year when it is divisible by four, with the exception that century years are not leap years unless they are also divisible by four hundred. As a single condition, a year is leap when it is divisible by four and not divisible by one hundred, or when it is divisible by four hundred. The flowchart reads the year, evaluates that compound condition, and prints Leap Year or Not a Leap Year, and for two thousand, which is divisible by four hundred, the answer is Leap Year.

The reason this matters in banking is the day-count convention for interest. Under an actual-days convention, a leap year has three hundred sixty-six days and a normal year three hundred sixty-five, and that denominator directly changes the interest figure, so getting leap-year detection wrong misprices interest. The century-year rule is the classic trap, because nineteen hundred is not a leap year but two thousand is, and it is very easy to implement the exceptions incorrectly or to get the operator precedence wrong. For that reason, while I can write the explicit condition, in production I delegate to the standard library's Year isLeap method, which implements the exact Gregorian rule, and I keep the explicit form alongside with an assertion so the two agree.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this fed the interest engine's day-count logic. I wrote a LeapYearService whose isLeapYear method computes the explicit condition, cross-checks it against Year isLeap, and returns the authoritative result, and the engine then used three hundred sixty-six days for leap years and three hundred sixty-five otherwise. For the year two thousand the service correctly reported a leap year and the interest used three hundred sixty-six days. The lesson I carry is that date rules are deceptively tricky, so for anything that touches money I lean on the battle-tested standard library rather than hand-rolled modulo logic.
